question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2021, agronomist Idris Hollenbeck claimed that maize grown in alternating rows with the Karsten bean variety yields more grain per hectare than maize grown alone, because the bean roots enrich the surrounding soil with nitrogen.
• A team led by Tavarri Vossberg at the Yarrowdale Field Research Station planted 12 plots of maize alternating with Karsten beans and 12 plots of maize alone, each plot measuring 6 meters by 10 meters.
• At harvest, the team weighed the grain from the maize rows in every plot.
• Maize in the alternating-row plots yielded an average of 9.1 metric tons of grain per hectare; maize in the plots without beans yielded an average of 7.4.
• At the midpoint of the growing season, the team also took soil cores 20 centimeters deep beside the maize rows in every plot and measured the total nitrogen in each core.
• The soil beside maize in the alternating-row plots held an average of 1.42 grams of nitrogen per kilogram of soil; the soil beside maize in the plots without beans held an average of 1.43.
• All 24 plots shared one field, and the maize in every plot was sown on the same day.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Hollenbeck's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings bear out Hollenbeck's observation but not his explanation: maize alternating with Karsten beans yielded an average of 9.1 metric tons of grain per hectare to 7.4 for maize alone, yet soil beside the maize held about the same nitrogen, 1.42 grams per kilogram versus 1.43.
answer_b: The team's findings undermine Hollenbeck's claim: soil beside the maize rows held about the same amount of nitrogen in the plots with beans as in the plots without them, an average of 1.42 grams per kilogram versus 1.43.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Hollenbeck's claim: maize grown in alternating rows with Karsten beans yielded an average of 9.1 metric tons of grain per hectare, compared with an average of 7.4 for maize grown alone.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Hollenbeck's claim and show the plots were otherwise comparable: maize alternating with Karsten beans yielded an average of 9.1 metric tons of grain per hectare to 7.4 for maize alone, and soil nitrogen was about the same, 1.42 grams per kilogram versus 1.43.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it matches each part of Hollenbeck's claim to the data that bears on it. Hollenbeck's sentence makes two assertions: that maize grown in alternating rows with the bean yields more grain per hectare than maize grown alone, and that this happens because the bean roots enrich the surrounding soil with nitrogen. The harvest data bear on the first assertion. Maize in the alternating-row plots averaged 9.1 metric tons per hectare compared with 7.4 for maize alone, so the higher yield Hollenbeck described did appear. The soil-core measurement bears on the second assertion, because the total nitrogen in soil beside the maize rows indicates whether the beans left that soil richer in nitrogen. At mid-season the soil beside maize with beans held 1.42 grams of nitrogen per kilogram and the soil beside maize alone held 1.43, so the data show no sign that the beans enriched the soil. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the number and size of the plots and the shared field and sowing date describe the study's method and do not bear on either assertion.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The nearly equal soil-nitrogen values (1.42 versus 1.43 grams per kilogram) do count against Hollenbeck's explanation, but the claim also says that maize with beans yields more grain per hectare, and the harvest results (9.1 versus 7.4 metric tons) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 9.1 versus 7.4 yields do fit the first part of Hollenbeck's claim, but Hollenbeck also said the higher yield happens because the bean roots enrich the soil with nitrogen, and the soil-nitrogen measurements (1.42 versus 1.43 grams per kilogram) show no sign of such enrichment. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the soil-nitrogen result as a check on the plots rather than a test of the explanation. It cites the right numbers, but the soil-nitrogen measurement is not a control showing that the plots were otherwise alike. It bears directly on Hollenbeck's 'because' clause, and the near-equal values (1.42 versus 1.43) show no sign that the beans enriched the soil with nitrogen, so the explanation is not borne out. Treating that result as strengthening the claim, rather than failing one part of it, is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the whole claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2021, educational psychologist Tamsin Vaelhorn claimed that students who take lecture notes by hand score higher on later conceptual questions than students who type their notes, because writing by hand is slower and so forces students to put ideas in their own words.
• A team led by Corwin Pennyfeather at the Dunmorrow Learning Laboratory had 90 undergraduates hear the same 40-minute recorded lecture, 45 taking notes by hand and 45 typing them.
• Two days later, each student answered 20 conceptual questions that required applying the lecture's ideas to situations the lecture had not described.
• The students who had taken notes by hand answered an average of 14.2 of the 20 questions correctly; the students who had typed answered an average of 12.4.
• In a separate analysis, the team compared each student's notes with the lecture transcript and calculated the percentage of note words that fell within runs of three or more consecutive words copied exactly from the lecturer.
• For the students who took notes by hand, 24 percent of note words fell within such runs; for the students who typed, the figure was also 24 percent.
• All students were tested individually in a seminar room, and none had studied the lecture's subject before.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Vaelhorn's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Vaelhorn's claim: the share of note words that fell within runs of three or more words copied exactly from the lecturer was 24 percent for the students who took notes by hand and 24 percent for the students who typed.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Vaelhorn's claim: the students who took notes by hand answered an average of 14.2 of the 20 conceptual questions correctly, compared with an average of 12.4 for the students who typed their notes.
answer_c: The team's findings support the score difference Vaelhorn claimed but not her account of why it arises: the students who took notes by hand averaged 14.2 of 20 questions correct to the typists' 12.4, yet 24 percent of note words fell within copied runs in both groups.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out and strengthen Vaelhorn's claim: the students who took notes by hand averaged 14.2 of 20 questions correct to the typists' 12.4, and the 24 percent of note words within copied runs in both groups shows the two groups were otherwise comparable.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it matches each part of Vaelhorn's claim to the data that bears on it. Her sentence makes two assertions: that students who take notes by hand score higher on later conceptual questions, and that this happens because writing by hand is slower and so forces students to put ideas in their own words. The conceptual-question results bear on the first assertion. The students who took notes by hand averaged 14.2 of 20 correct, compared with 12.4 for the students who typed, so the higher scores she described did appear. The analysis of the notes bears on the second assertion, because the share of note words falling within runs of three or more words copied exactly from the lecturer is a measure of how much students were reproducing the lecturer's phrasing rather than restating ideas in their own words. If handwriting forced restating, the handwritten notes should contain a smaller share of copied wording. Instead, the share was 24 percent for both groups, so the notes show no difference in how much wording was copied. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the number of students, the lecture's length, the testing setting, and students' prior knowledge describe the method and do not bear on either assertion.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one measure. The identical 24 percent figures do count against Vaelhorn's explanation, but her claim also says that students who take notes by hand score higher on later conceptual questions, and the results of 14.2 versus 12.4 questions correct are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part of a claim and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one measure. The 14.2 versus 12.4 averages do fit the first part of Vaelhorn's claim, that handwriting students score higher, but she also said this happens because handwriting forces students to put ideas in their own words, and the notes analysis (24 percent copied wording in both groups) shows no such difference. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part of a claim and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads what the notes analysis shows. It cites the right numbers, but the 24 percent figure for both groups is not a check that the groups were otherwise comparable; it is a measure of the thing Vaelhorn's explanation depends on, namely how much of the lecturer's exact phrasing students reproduced. Identical shares mean handwriting did not reduce copying, which fails to support her explanation rather than strengthening her claim. This is the pattern of treating a null result on the mechanism measure as a control that confirms the claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2021, physiologist Torvald Oskarsen claimed that adults who swim outdoors in cold water throughout the winter catch fewer colds than adults who do not, because repeated cold exposure raises the number of circulating white blood cells.
• A team led by Mireille Ardoven at the Harlowe Institute for Human Biology followed 90 adults who swam outdoors at least three times a week from November through March and 90 adults who did not swim outdoors during that period.
• In January, each participant gave a small blood sample, and the team counted the cells in it using an automated analyzer.
• The swimmers averaged 7,400 white blood cells per microliter of blood; the non-swimmers averaged 5,900.
• Throughout the winter, each participant recorded every cold, defined as two or more days of runny nose, sore throat, or cough, in a daily symptom diary.
• The swimmers reported an average of 2.3 colds over the winter; the non-swimmers also reported an average of 2.3.
• Participants in both groups lived within 40 kilometers of the institute, and the diaries were collected in April.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Oskarsen's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine what Oskarsen claimed about white blood cells: the swimmers and the non-swimmers each reported an average of 2.3 colds over the winter.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Oskarsen's claim: the swimmers averaged 7,400 white blood cells per microliter of blood, compared with an average of 5,900 for the non-swimmers.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out the effect Oskarsen described but not the cause he gave for it: the swimmers and the non-swimmers each reported an average of 2.3 colds over the winter, yet the swimmers averaged 7,400 white blood cells per microliter of blood to the non-swimmers' 5,900.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out the physiological difference Oskarsen cited but not the effect he attributed to it: the swimmers averaged 7,400 white blood cells per microliter of blood to the non-swimmers' 5,900, yet both groups reported an average of 2.3 colds over the winter.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it matches each part of Oskarsen's claim to the data that bears on it. Oskarsen's sentence says two things: that adults who swim outdoors in cold water through the winter catch fewer colds, and that this happens because repeated cold exposure raises the number of circulating white blood cells. The diary records bear on the first part. The swimmers reported an average of 2.3 colds over the winter and the non-swimmers also reported an average of 2.3, so the swimmers did not catch fewer colds. The blood counts bear on the second part, because they directly measure the number of circulating white blood cells. The swimmers averaged 7,400 cells per microliter of blood and the non-swimmers averaged 5,900, so the swimmers did have more circulating white blood cells, as Oskarsen said. The team's findings therefore bear out the physiological difference Oskarsen cited but not the reduction in colds he attributed to it. The notes about where participants lived and when the diaries were collected describe the study's method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it uses the cold counts to judge the wrong part of Oskarsen's claim. The identical cold counts (2.3 for both groups) bear on whether swimmers catch fewer colds; they say nothing about white blood cells. The measure that does bear on white blood cells is the blood count, and there the swimmers averaged 7,400 cells per microliter to the non-swimmers' 5,900, which is consistent with what Oskarsen said about white blood cells rather than undermining it. This is the pattern of matching a data note to a part of the claim it does not measure.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one measure. The higher white blood cell counts match the cause Oskarsen cited, but the claim is about catching fewer colds, and the swimmers and non-swimmers each reported an average of 2.3 colds, so the effect he described did not appear.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it reverses which part of Oskarsen's claim each result supports. It cites the right numbers, but the conclusion is backward. The identical cold counts (2.3 for both groups) show that swimmers did not catch fewer colds, so the effect Oskarsen described did not appear. The higher white blood cell counts (7,400 versus 5,900 per microliter) are consistent with the physiological difference he cited, so that part is not undermined. This is the pattern of swapping which part of a claim the data supports and which it does not.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2022, consumer-behavior researcher Ishbel Corrowby claimed that cafés that print calorie counts on their menu boards sell fewer pastries than cafés that do not, because seeing the counts makes customers more aware of how many calories a pastry contains.
• A team led by Yusuf Tarnoway at the Kellowick Food Behavior Laboratory compared 24 cafés of the Pemberly Lane chain that print counts on their menu boards with 24 Pemberly Lane cafés that do not.
• Using till records over 28 consecutive days, the team found that the cafés with printed counts sold an average of 94 pastries per day, while the cafés without printed counts sold an average of 118.
• In a separate exit survey, 300 customers at each kind of café were asked, as they left the counter, to state how many calories a croissant on display contained. The same croissant was sold at all 48 cafés, and at the cafés with printed counts its calorie count appeared on the menu board.
• The team then recorded how far each customer's answer was from the croissant's actual calorie content.
• Customers at the cafés with printed counts were off by an average of 142 calories; customers at the cafés without printed counts were off by an average of 141 calories.
• The surveys were conducted on weekday mornings between 7 and 10 a.m.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Corrowby's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Corrowby's claim: customers at the cafés with printed counts were off by an average of 142 calories in estimating the croissant, and customers at the cafés without printed counts were off by an average of 141 calories.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Corrowby's claim: the cafés with printed counts sold an average of 94 pastries per day, compared with an average of 118 per day at the cafés without printed counts.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Corrowby's observation but not her explanation: the cafés with printed counts sold an average of 94 pastries per day to the others' 118, yet customers at the two kinds of café were off by nearly the same amount, 142 calories versus 141.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Corrowby's claim and strengthen it: the cafés with printed counts sold an average of 94 pastries per day to the others' 118, and customers at the two kinds of café were off by nearly the same amount, 142 calories versus 141, so the sales gap can be traced to the counts.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it matches each part of Corrowby's claim to the data that bears on it. Her sentence makes two separate assertions: that cafés with printed calorie counts sell fewer pastries, and that this happens because the counts make customers more aware of how many calories a pastry contains. The till records bear on the first assertion. The cafés with printed counts sold an average of 94 pastries per day and the cafés without them sold an average of 118, so the lower pastry sales she described did appear. The exit survey bears on the second assertion, although the notes never describe it in her terms. If seeing the counts made customers more aware of how many calories a pastry contains, customers who had just ordered at cafés with the croissant's count on the board should have judged its calorie content more accurately, and their answers should have missed by less. Instead they were off by an average of 142 calories, compared with 141 at the cafés without counts, so there is no sign that the counts left customers better informed. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about how the surveys were timed describe the study's method and bear on neither part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one measure. The nearly equal estimation errors (142 versus 141 calories) do count against Corrowby's explanation, but her claim also says that cafés with printed counts sell fewer pastries, and the till records (94 versus 118 pastries per day) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one measure. The 94 versus 118 pastries per day do fit the first part of Corrowby's claim, but she also said the gap arises because the counts make customers more aware of the calories in a pastry, and the survey errors (142 versus 141 calories) show no sign of that greater awareness. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the survey result as a point in the claim's favor. The nearly equal errors (142 versus 141 calories) are not a check showing that the two kinds of café were otherwise alike. The survey measures how well customers could judge a pastry's calorie content, which is exactly what Corrowby's explanation depends on, and the equal errors show the counts did not improve that. The sales gap is therefore not traced to the counts by these findings. This is the pattern of treating data that fails a mechanism as a control that strengthens the whole claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2008, economic historian Gwenllian Ashmoor claimed that the weekly market in the river town of Ostbury grew larger after a stone bridge was built across the River Tarrel in 1262, because the bridge drew traders from the villages on the far bank.
• A team led by Selwyn Corrigan at the Aldcastle Archaeological Unit excavated the market square and compared the layers laid down before 1262 with those laid down after it.
• In the earlier layers, the team identified 41 sets of post-holes marking separate stall plots; in the later layers, it identified 67.
• The team also sorted the pottery sherds recovered from the market layers by clay composition, which can be matched to the kilns that supplied each vessel. Traders from the far-bank villages sold mostly pottery made at far-bank kilns. In the earlier layers, 24 percent of sherds came from kilns on the far bank; in the later layers, 24 percent did.
• The excavated area covered the same stretch of the square in both periods, and the team recovered 1,150 sherds in total.
• Excavation lasted two summer seasons.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Ashmoor's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Ashmoor's claim: the share of sherds from far-bank kilns was 24 percent in the earlier layers and 24 percent in the later layers.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Ashmoor's observation but not her explanation: the number of stall plots rose from 41 to 67, yet the share of sherds from far-bank kilns was 24 percent in both the earlier and later layers.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Ashmoor's claim: the number of stall plots rose from 41 in the earlier layers to 67 in the later layers.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Ashmoor's claim and add to it: the number of stall plots rose from 41 to 67, and the share of sherds from far-bank kilns held at 24 percent in both periods as the market expanded.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it matches each part of Ashmoor's claim to the data that bears on it. Ashmoor's sentence says two things: that the market grew larger after the bridge was built, and that it did so because the bridge drew traders from the far-bank villages. The stall-plot count bears on the first part. The earlier layers held 41 sets of post-holes and the later layers held 67, so the market did grow. The pottery analysis bears on the second part, even though the notes never use the word traders. The notes say that traders from the far-bank villages sold mostly pottery made at far-bank kilns, and the sherds' clay can be matched to the kilns that made them. If many more traders had come from the far-bank villages, far-bank vessels should have made up a larger share of the sherds after 1262. Instead the share was 24 percent in both periods, so the pottery gives no sign that far-bank traders accounted for the market's growth; if they had, the far-bank share should have risen. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the excavated area, the total sherds, and the length of the excavation describe the study's method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical far-bank sherd shares (24 percent in both periods) do count against Ashmoor's explanation, but she also claimed that the market grew larger, and the rise in stall plots from 41 to 67 is consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The rise from 41 to 67 stall plots fits the first part of Ashmoor's claim, that the market grew larger, but she also said this happened because the bridge drew far-bank traders, and a larger share of far-bank pottery would be expected if that were so. The share stayed at 24 percent. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the unchanged pottery share as extra support. A steady 24 percent may mean that far-bank goods kept pace with a larger market, but it does not show that far-bank traders caused the growth, which is what Ashmoor's explanation requires; if they had, the far-bank share should have risen. The numbers are accurate, but the findings do not add support to her claim. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism measure as confirmation.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2021, glaciologist Halla Valtorsen claimed that the Karsholt Glacier lost thickness faster in 2011–2020 than in 2001–2010, because windblown dark dust that settled on its surface made the ice absorb more sunlight.
• A team led by Maren Brekkvold at the Pellinore Alpine Research Station analyzed records from 40 survey stakes drilled into the glacier's surface, which were re-measured each September by the same two-person crew.
• The stakes showed average thinning of 1.18 meters per year in 2011–2020, compared with 0.62 meters per year in 2001–2010.
• The team also used satellite images to measure the fraction of incoming sunlight that the glacier's surface reflected back to space during the July–August melt season.
• In 2001–2010, the surface reflected an average of 0.31 of the incoming sunlight.
• In 2011–2020, the surface reflected an average of 0.31 of the incoming sunlight.
• The amount of incoming sunlight during July–August was about the same in both decades, and most of the glacier's yearly melting happens in those months.
• Both sets of satellite images were taken from the same orbit, at about the same time of day.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Valtorsen's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Valtorsen's claim: the glacier's surface reflected an average of 0.31 of the incoming sunlight in 2001–2010 and an average of 0.31 in 2011–2020.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Valtorsen's claim: the glacier thinned by an average of 1.18 meters per year in 2011–2020, compared with an average of 0.62 meters per year in 2001–2010.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Valtorsen's claim and show that nothing else about the surface changed: the glacier thinned by an average of 1.18 meters per year in 2011–2020 versus 0.62 meters per year in 2001–2010, while its surface reflected an average of 0.31 of the incoming sunlight in both decades.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Valtorsen's observation but not her explanation: the glacier thinned by an average of 1.18 meters per year in 2011–2020 versus 0.62 meters per year in 2001–2010, yet its surface reflected an average of 0.31 of the incoming sunlight in both decades.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it matches each part of Valtorsen's claim to the data that bears on it. Her sentence makes two assertions: that the Karsholt Glacier lost thickness faster in 2011–2020 than in 2001–2010, and that this happened because windblown dark dust made the ice absorb more sunlight. The survey-stake records bear on the first assertion. Average thinning was 1.18 meters per year in 2011–2020 versus 0.62 meters per year in 2001–2010, so the faster loss she described did occur. The satellite measurement bears on the second assertion, although the notes never describe it in her terms. Sunlight that reaches the surface is either reflected or taken in by the ice, so if the surface sent back the same fraction of about the same amount of incoming sunlight in both decades (0.31), it took in about the same amount in both decades. That is not the increase in sunlight taken in that her explanation requires. The findings therefore bear out the observation but count against the explanation. The notes about the stake crew and the satellite orbit describe the study's method and do not bear on either assertion.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one measurement. The identical reflected fractions (0.31 in both decades) do count against Valtorsen's explanation, but her claim also says the glacier thinned faster in 2011–2020, and the stake records (1.18 versus 0.62 meters per year) show that it did. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part of a claim and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one measurement. The stake records (1.18 versus 0.62 meters per year) fit the first part of Valtorsen's claim, but she also said the faster thinning happened because the ice took in more sunlight, and a surface that reflected 0.31 of incoming sunlight in both decades did not take in more. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part of a claim and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it misreads the satellite measurement as a control showing that the surface stayed otherwise unchanged. The identical reflected fractions (0.31 in both decades) do not show that nothing else about the surface changed, and if the surface had not changed, dust could not have darkened it, so that reading contradicts the very explanation D says is borne out. The measurement bears on Valtorsen's explanation, and it shows no increase in how much sunlight the ice took in. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the proposed mechanism as confirmation of the whole claim.
